about: Sections of an essay on romance by Joel (first person). In each, the sentences listed under "changed" were just rewritten; the rest is the essay as it stands. Read each section as it stands, with its heading.

texts.heading: Spirituality to bypass intimacy
changed: Do you feel like you’re losing some control, and does that scare you?
sentences: I’ve used spirituality as a replacement for intimacy a lot because intimacy was simply unavailable.
As a boy and young man, I was so deprived of female touch that it was driving me insane.
Meditation sometimes helped me cope better with the deprivation, but it wasn’t a cure.
I remember once as I was entering into an ayahuasca ego death, I said, “Actually, I really just want a girlfriend.”
Right then, the crazy trip abruptly ended, and a voice said, “Ok then go find one.”
Nobody believes this story when I tell it.
I don’t believe most people can be truly happy celibate.
People generally aren’t so serious about spiritual liberation that giving up sex and partnership for life makes sense.
The Buddha didn’t advise everyone to become monastics.
If becoming a monastic genuinely makes you happier and more peaceful, stay.
It might work for some very advanced people, or if your sexual desire is already low, or you’re old, etc.
But how do you know what you’re not aware of?
Inner-child reparenting and self-hypnosis can help a lot with that, because often the inner child is being ignored while the adult is feeling some kind of liberation.
And if you’re so happy and free, what happens when you’re alone in a room with a super beautiful girl and she wants you?
Or vice versa for women.
Do you feel like you’re losing some control, and does that scare you?

texts.heading: The conversation about flaws
changed: I’d want both of us to be honest about how well we actually handle our own issues, starting with which addictions or impulsive behaviors we can’t reliably control.
Answers like those tell me more than either of us proclaiming that we’re healed.
sentences: Card games and social gatherings don’t tell you everything, but asking someone out of the blue, “What did you do wrong in your past relationships?” would make for a pretty weird date.
At the right time, though, in the right way (especially if they bring it up tangentially), I would ask about their past relationships, especially the recent ones.
If every story ends with everything being the other person’s fault, I’d ask, “Okay, so what lessons did you find for yourself?”
“I have baggage” isn't as useful as learning what you're having trouble with now.
What might make it hard for you to function well in a relationship?
I’d want both of us to be honest about how well we actually handle our own issues, starting with which addictions or impulsive behaviors we can’t reliably control.
What are we probably going to ask forgiveness for more than once?
Answers like those tell me more than either of us proclaiming that we’re healed.
Look at the most recent conflicts and ask if you were able to regulate yourself during them.
What did you do to the other person, and how did you repair the damage afterward?
Not doing can be just as bad as overdoing.
If conflict makes you shut down, does it mean you stop talking to your partner for days, leaving them feeling abandoned?
Has your judgment gotten better, or would your friends or exes say you keep falling for the same stuff?

texts.heading: Beware idealization in either direction
changed: You know how it goes: “We’re twin flames!” or “I’m Lord Krishna and she’s Radha!”

For example, I still love women I’ve loved before, and sometimes I talk about them, with no intention of making my current partner jealous, just because I’m thinking about them and I don’t want to hide it.
sentences: When the BPD splitting kicks in, she goes from “you’re perfect” to “you’re a fraud,” first in private and then in front of everybody.
Suddenly she can see every flaw I have, and decides I was faking it all along.
Sometimes she ends up accusing me of thinking I’m perfect, when she’s the one who used to say I was.
I’ve learned to get nervous when somebody "knows" too much about me/us too soon.
You know how it goes: “We’re twin flames!” or “I’m Lord Krishna and she’s Radha!”
Okay, maybe I really am way better than the other guys she’s found.
But if she hasn’t found anything about me that bothers her yet, she hasn’t found all of me.

For example, I still love women I’ve loved before, and sometimes I talk about them, with no intention of making my current partner jealous, just because I’m thinking about them and I don’t want to hide it.
If she can’t handle the truth that I still love them, she isn’t ready for me.
If she says, “Can you talk less about your exes?”
Well, yes, I'll happily oblige, since maybe I do talk about them too much sometimes.
But I'm hoping that doesn't mean she also wants to pretend I'm not thinking of them just because I don't blast it out loud.
And I also can't stand the double standard if she's talking about her exes while I can't talk about mine.

texts.heading: From flow to nitty gritty
changed: Living alone is easy in so many ways, like I can make my bed whenever I want.

That freedom works wonderfully until I’m in a romantic relationship, and suddenly I’m expected to read her mind, silences included, and check in constantly, and then I’m not allowed to use all that expert “management” to manipulate her.
sentences: Living alone is easy in so many ways, like I can make my bed whenever I want.
When I have a girlfriend, making the bed in the morning can become one of the ways I show her I love her.
If I don’t do it well, somehow it may become a bad omen that I don’t care about her, which is a lot of emotional weight for a bed.
Dealing with somebody else’s emotional insecurities can also be exhausting.
It’s easy to feel free when I don’t have to do that, especially since I’m a bit of an introvert and 10% autistic.

That freedom works wonderfully until I’m in a romantic relationship, and suddenly I’m expected to read her mind, silences included, and check in constantly, and then I’m not allowed to use all that expert “management” to manipulate her.

texts.heading: Muses & Directors
changed: I don’t think that goes against equality, since equality doesn’t have to mean dividing every role 50/50.
If I like driving and for her it’s cooking, great, and whatever she’s way better at, she’ll probably do more of.
Even when I’m the one leading, I still want to know what she sees.
sentences: In my experience, women often prefer me to say directly:
“This is where I want to go.
This is what I think we should do.
Are you game?”
She might have a better idea, or just not want to do it, but she still wants me to take initiative.
I don’t think that goes against equality, since equality doesn’t have to mean dividing every role 50/50.
If I like driving and for her it’s cooking, great, and whatever she’s way better at, she’ll probably do more of.
Even when I’m the one leading, I still want to know what she sees.
Mandar obedeciendo—Lead by following—as the Zapatistas say.

texts.heading: Which marriage vows are honest?
changed: Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it, and that if you then tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, God will be angry and destroy your work.
sentences: Conventional marriage vows are dishonest and inept, and most people know it.
You can’t promise how you’ll feel in the future, but you can promise actions if you really believe you’re capable of delivering them.
So for example, you could promise to tell the truth, to keep showing up emotionally, to support the children, or whatever else you genuinely believe you can do even if your feelings change.

More importantly, though, if you do keep those promises, it's quite likely that your connection will deepen, so it's not like we truly have no control of future feelings, but just not completely, directly or unilaterally.
We also find something like my warning in the New & Old Testaments.

Ecclesiastes 5:4–6 says it is better not to make a vow than to make one and fail to keep it, and that if you then tell the priest you didn’t mean what you promised, God will be angry and destroy your work.
Matthew 5:33–37 and James 5:12 make the wedding vow itself look even more suspicious (to me, anyway): let your “Yes” be “Yes” and your “No” be “No,” and anything beyond that comes from evil.
Where did the idea of promising to have romantic interest in your partner come from, anyway?
It turns out it never existed in any culture I’m aware of until the 19th century, when people in England began citing romance as their reason for marriage.
That trend has continued evolving like a snowball until today.
But what our ancestors knew was not wrong: You can sign a contract about what you’ll do, but feelings aren’t contractual.

texts.heading: If you’re already in it
changed: That drove me crazy, because why would she lie like that?
sentences: Most of this article is about what to do before jumping head first into head over shoulders.
But if you’re already married with children, advice about slowing down arrives a little late.
I wish I had a special method for fixing that.
Mostly I learned the obvious thing the hard way: one person can’t fix the relationship (unless they’re the main problem in it).
With Bee and Key, the biggest thing sitting underneath everything was trust.
They wanted to be with me and would say they trusted me, but really they didn’t trust me, themself, or anyone else.
It was all or nothing: blind trust, or none.
I kept saying, “It’s not possible to have a relationship without trust.”
I think that rigidity came from trauma and never really growing up.
Even dishonesty was sometimes hard for me to define in these relationships.
Bee once opened a door and, a second later, said she hadn’t opened it.
That drove me crazy, because why would she lie like that?
On the other hand, although she was technically lying, there was no strategy behind it, and she was usually quite honest.
Non-strategic lying is literally defined as "pathological lying," so I should have seen it more like an illness than a failure of virtue.
